questions.stem:
A rough plane is inclined to the horizontal at an angle $\alpha$, where $\tan\alpha = \frac{3}{4}$
A brick $P$ of mass $m$ is placed on the plane.
The coefficient of friction between $P$ and the plane is $\mu$
Brick $P$ is in equilibrium and on the point of sliding down the plane.
Brick $P$ is modelled as a particle.
Using the model,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) find, in terms of $m$ and $g$, the magnitude of the normal reaction of the plane on brick $P$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: Resolve perpendicular to the plane
A1: $R = mg\cos\alpha = \frac{4}{5}mg$
(2)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Correct no. of terms, condone sin/cos confusion
- A1: cao with no wrong working seen. $mg\cos36.86$ is A0

parts.label: b
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: Resolve parallel to the plane or horizontally or vertically
A1: $F = mg\sin\alpha$ or $R\sin\alpha = F\cos\alpha$
M1: Use $F = \mu R$ and solve for $\mu$
A1*: $\mu = \frac{3}{4}$*
(4)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Correct no. of terms, condone sin/cos confusion
- M1: Must use $F = \mu R$ (not merely state it) to obtain a numerical value for $\mu$. This is an independent M mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
For parts (c) and (d), you are not required to do any further calculations.
Brick $P$ is now removed from the plane and a much heavier brick $Q$ is placed on the plane.
The coefficient of friction between $Q$ and the plane is also $\frac{3}{4}$
(c) Explain briefly why brick $Q$ will remain at rest on the plane.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) B1: The forces acting on $Q$ will still balance as the $m$'s cancel oe
Other possibilities:
e.g. the friction will increase in the same proportion as the weight component or force down the plane.
The force pulling the brick down the plane increases by the same amount as the friction oe
This mark can be scored if they do the calculation.
(1)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1: Must have the 3 underlined phrases/word oe

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Brick $Q$ is now projected with speed $0.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ down a line of greatest slope of the plane.
Brick $Q$ is modelled as a particle.
Using the model,
(d) describe the motion of brick $Q$, giving a reason for your answer.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) B1: Brick $Q$ slides down the plane with constant speed.
B1: No resultant force down the plane (so no acceleration) oe
These marks can be scored if they do the calculation.
(2)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1: Must say constant speed.
- B1: Any appropriate equivalent statement

questions.stem:
A particle $P$ moves with acceleration $(4\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
At time $t = 0$, $P$ is moving with velocity $(-2\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the velocity of $P$ at time $t = 2$ seconds.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: Use of $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$ or integrate to give: $\mathbf{v} = (-2\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) + 2(4\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})$
A1: $(6\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j})\,(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})$
(2)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: For any complete method to give a $\mathbf{v}$ expression with correct no. of terms with $t = 2$ used, so if integrating, must see the initial velocity as the constant. Allow sign errors.
- A1: Cao isw if they go on to find the speed.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
At time $t = 0$, $P$ passes through the origin $O$.
At time $t = T$ seconds, where $T > 0$, the particle $P$ passes through the point $A$.
The position vector of $A$ is $(\lambda\mathbf{i} - 4.5\mathbf{j})\mathrm{m}$ relative to $O$, where $\lambda$ is a constant.
(b) Find the value of $T$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: Solve problem through use of $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{u}t + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ or integration (M0 if $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$)
Or any other complete method e.g. use $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}T$ and $\mathbf{r} = \frac{(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})T}{2}$:
A1: $-4.5\mathbf{j} = 2t\mathbf{j} - \frac{1}{2}t^2 5\mathbf{j}$ ($\mathbf{j}$ terms only)
The first two marks could be implied if they go straight to an algebraic equation.
M1: Attempt to equate $\mathbf{j}$ components to give equation in $T$ only $(-4.5 = 2T - \frac{5}{2}T^2)$
A1: $T = 1.8$
(4)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: For any complete method to give a vector expression for $\mathbf{j}$ component of displacement in $t$ (or $T$) only, using $\mathbf{a} = (4\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})$, so if integrating, RHS of equation must have the correct structure. Allow sign errors.
- A1: Correct $\mathbf{j}$ vector equation in $t$ or $T$. Ignore $\mathbf{i}$ terms.
- M1: Must have earned 1st M mark. Equate $\mathbf{j}$ components to give equation in $T$ (allow $t$) only (no $\mathbf{j}$'s) which has come from a displacement. Equation must be a 3 term quadratic in $T$.

parts.label: c
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: Solve problem by substituting their $T$ value (M0 if $T < 0$) into the $\mathbf{i}$ component equation to give an equation in $\lambda$ only: $\lambda = -2T + \frac{1}{2}T^2 \times 4$
A1: $\lambda = 2.9$ or $2.88$ or $\frac{72}{25}$ oe
(2)
Notes: Accept column vectors throughout
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Must have earned 1st M mark in (b) Complete method - must have an equation in $\lambda$ only (no $\mathbf{i}$'s) which has come from an appropriate displacement.. (e.g M0 if $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}$ has been used) Expression for $\lambda$ must be a quadratic in $T$

parts.label: i(a)
parts.text:
(i) At time $t$ seconds, where $t \geqslant 0$, a particle $P$ moves so that its acceleration $\mathbf{a}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ is given by
$\mathbf{a} = (1 - 4t)\mathbf{i} + (3 - t^2)\mathbf{j}$
At the instant when $t = 0$, the velocity of $P$ is $36\mathbf{i}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
(a) Find the velocity of $P$ when $t = 4$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(i)(a) M1: Integrate $\mathbf{a}$ wrt $t$ to obtain velocity
A1: $\mathbf{v} = (t - 2t^2)\mathbf{i} + \left(3t - \frac{1}{3}t^3\right)\mathbf{j}\ (+\mathbf{C})$
A1: $8\mathbf{i} - \frac{28}{3}\mathbf{j}\ (\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})$
(3)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: At least 3 terms with powers increasing by 1 (but M0 if clearly just multiplying by $t$)
- A1: Accept $8\mathbf{i} - 9.3\mathbf{j}$ or better. Isw if speed found.

parts.label: i(b)
parts.text:
(b) Find the value of $t$ at the instant when $P$ is moving in a direction perpendicular to $\mathbf{i}$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(i)(b) M1: Equate $\mathbf{i}$ component of $\mathbf{v}$ to zero
A1ft: $t - 2t^2 + 36 = 0$
A1: $t = 4.5$ (ignore an incorrect second solution)
(3)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Must have an equation in $t$ only (Must have integrated to find a velocity vector)
- A1ft: Correct equation follow through on their $\mathbf{v}$ but must be a 3 term quadratic

parts.label: ii
parts.text:
(ii) At time $t$ seconds, where $t \geqslant 0$, a particle $Q$ moves so that its position vector $\mathbf{r}$ metres, relative to a fixed origin $O$, is given by
$\mathbf{r} = (t^2 - t)\mathbf{i} + 3t\mathbf{j}$
Find the value of $t$ at the instant when the speed of $Q$ is $5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
(ii) M1: Differentiate $\mathbf{r}$ wrt to $t$ to obtain velocity
A1: $\mathbf{v} = (2t - 1)\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}$
M1: Use magnitude to give an equation in $t$ only
A1: $(2t - 1)^2 + 3^2 = 5^2$
M1: Solve problem by solving this equation for $t$
A1: $t = 2.5$
(6)
Notes: Accept column vectors throughout
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: At least 2 terms with powers decreasing by 1 (but M0 if clearly just dividing by $t$)
- M1: Use magnitude to give an equation in $t$ only, must have differentiated to find a velocity (M0 if they use $\sqrt{x^2 - y^2}$)
- A1: Correct equation $\sqrt{(2t-1)^2 + 3^2} = 5$
- M1: Solve a 3 term quadratic for $t$ which has come from differentiating and using a magnitude. This M mark can be implied by a correct answer with no working.

questions.stem:
A ladder $AB$ has mass $M$ and length $6a$.
The end $A$ of the ladder is on rough horizontal ground.
The ladder rests against a fixed smooth horizontal rail at the point $C$.
The point $C$ is at a vertical height $4a$ above the ground.
The vertical plane containing $AB$ is perpendicular to the rail.
The ladder is inclined to the horizontal at an angle $\alpha$, where $\sin\alpha = \frac{4}{5}$, as shown in Figure 1.
The coefficient of friction between the ladder and the ground is $\mu$.
The ladder rests in limiting equilibrium.
The ladder is modelled as a uniform rod.
Using the model,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) show that the magnitude of the force exerted on the ladder by the rail at $C$ is $\frac{9Mg}{25}$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: Take moments about $A$
A1: $N \times \frac{4a}{\sin\alpha} = Mg \times 3a\cos\alpha$
A1*: $\frac{9Mg}{25}$*
(3)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Correct no. of terms, dim correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors for an equation in $N$ and $Mg$ only. For perp distance allow any of : $\frac{4a}{\sin\alpha}, \frac{4a}{\cos\alpha}, 5a$ but use of any of : $6a, 5a\sin\alpha, 4a\cos\alpha$,.... or anything involving $\tan\alpha$ is M0 Also M0 if no $a$'s in their first equation.
- A1: Correct equation, trig does not need to be substituted

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Hence, or otherwise, find the value of $\mu$.
(7)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: Resolve horizontally
A1: $(\rightarrow) F = \frac{9Mg}{25}\sin\alpha$
M1: Resolve vertically
A1: $(\uparrow) R + \frac{9Mg}{25}\cos\alpha = Mg$
Other possible equations:
$(\nwarrow), R\cos\alpha + \frac{9Mg}{25} = Mg\cos\alpha + F\sin\alpha$
$(\nearrow), Mg\sin\alpha = F\cos\alpha + R\sin\alpha$
$\mathrm{M}(C), Mg.2a\cos\alpha + F.5a\sin\alpha = R.5a\cos\alpha$
$\mathrm{M}(G), \frac{9Mg}{25}.2a + F.3a\sin\alpha = R.3a\cos\alpha$
$\mathrm{M}(B), Mg.3a\cos\alpha + F.6a\sin\alpha = R.6a\cos\alpha + \frac{9Mg}{25}a$
$\left(F = \frac{36Mg}{125},\ R = \frac{98Mg}{125}\right)$
N.B. The above 4 marks are for any two equations, either resolutions or moments or one of each. Mark best two equations.
Equations may appear in part (a) but must be used in (b) to earn marks.
M1: $F = \mu R$ used. Must be used, e.g. seen on the diagram, i.e. M0 if merely quoting it. (M0 if $F = \mu \times \frac{9Mg}{25}$ used)
M1: Eliminate $R$ and $F$ and solve for $\mu$. Must have 3 equations (and all 3 previous M marks)
Alternative equations if they have at $A$: $X$ horizontally and $Y$ perpendicular to the rod.
$(\nwarrow), Y + \frac{9Mg}{25} = Mg\cos\alpha + X\sin\alpha$
$(\nearrow), Mg\sin\alpha = X\cos\alpha$
$(\uparrow), \frac{9Mg}{25}\cos\alpha + Y\cos\alpha = Mg$
$(\rightarrow), Y\sin\alpha + \frac{9Mg}{25}\sin\alpha = X$
$\mathrm{M}(C), Mg.2a\cos\alpha + X.5a\sin\alpha = Y.5a$
$\mathrm{M}(G), \frac{9Mg}{25}.2a + X.3a\sin\alpha = Y.3a$ M1A1 M1A1
$\mathrm{M}(B), Mg.3a\cos\alpha + X.6a\sin\alpha = Y.6a + \frac{9Mg}{25}a$
$\left(X = \frac{4Mg}{3},\ Y = \frac{98Mg}{75}\right)$
Then $F = \mu R$ becomes: $X - Y\sin\alpha = \mu Y\cos\alpha$ M1
Eliminate $X$ and $Y$ and solve for $\mu$ M1
A1: $\mu = \frac{18}{49}$ (0.3673.... accept 0.37 or better)
(7)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Correct no. of terms, dim correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors
- A1: Correct equation, trig does not need to be substituted but $N$ does.
- M1: Correct no. of terms, dim correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors

questions.stem:
A small ball is projected with speed $U\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ from a point $O$ at the top of a vertical cliff.
The point $O$ is $25\,\mathrm{m}$ vertically above the point $N$ which is on horizontal ground.
The ball is projected at an angle of $45°$ above the horizontal.
The ball hits the ground at a point $A$, where $AN = 100\,\mathrm{m}$, as shown in Figure 2.
The motion of the ball is modelled as that of a particle moving freely under gravity.
Using this initial model,

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: Using horizontal motion
A1: $U\cos45°\,t = 100$
M1: Using vertical motion
A1: $U\sin45°\,t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = -25$
M1: Solve problem by eliminating $t$ and solving for $U$
A1*: $U = 28$*
(6)

- A1*: Exact given answer correctly obtained with no wrong working (e.g. $g = 9.81$ used) or approximation seen.

parts.text:

(3)

(3)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
In a refinement to the model of the motion of the ball from $O$ to $A$, the effect of air resistance is included.
This refined model is used to find a new value of $U$.
(c) How would this new value of $U$ compare with 28, the value given in part (a)?
(1)

parts.text:
